items.name: EU Unfair Commercial Practices Directive 2005/29/EC as amended by the Omnibus Directive (EU) 2019/2161: misleading actions, misleading omissions and the Annex I blacklist
items.one_line: The EU's general ban on misleading and aggressive business-to-consumer marketing: true-but-misleading copy, hidden ads, missing price or trader information, fake 'free', bait offers, false countdowns, undisclosed paid ranking and fake or misrepresented reviews are unlawful in every Member State.

sources.title: EU Publications Office: Directive 2005/29/EC, consolidated text of 28.05.2022 (incorporating Directive (EU) 2019/2161)
sources.supports: Articles 6 and 7 (misleading actions and omissions, incl. new 7(4a) ranking and 7(6) reviews), Article 13 penalties, Annex I points 5, 7, 11, 11a, 17, 20, 22, 23b, 23c

sources.supports: transposition by 28 November 2021, application from 28 May 2022

sources.title: EU Publications Office: Directive (EU) 2024/825 (empowering consumers for the green transition), amending Directive 2005/29/EC
sources.supports: application from 27 September 2026; new Annex I points 2a (sustainability labels), 4a (generic environmental claims), 4b, 4c (offsetting-based neutral claims), 10a, 23d onwards

sources.supports: section 3.4 use of the claim 'free'; 4.2.4 user reviews (reasonable and proportionate steps, misrepresentation examples); 4.2.6 influencer marketing disclosure

items.note: Status as read 2026-10-13: in force; the consolidated text of 28.05.2022 lists one amendment, Directive (EU) 2019/2161, which Member States had to ‘apply those measures from 28 May 2022’ (2019/2161). RECENT CHANGE: Directive (EU) 2024/825 amends the UCPD again and Member States ‘shall apply those measures from 27 September 2026’ (2024/825); the consolidated text read does not yet include it. A directive works through each Member State's national law. Rules for a copywriter: (1) Misleading action: copy is misleading if it deceives ‘including overall presentation’, ‘even if the information is factually correct’, about e.g. the price, main characteristics or ‘the results to be expected from its use’ (Art 6(1), consolidated text). (2) Misleading omission: hiding material information or giving it ‘in an unclear, unintelligible, ambiguous or untimely manner’, or failing to identify commercial intent (Art 7(2)); an invitation to purchase must give the main characteristics, trader identity and address, and ‘the price inclusive of taxes’ plus delivery charges (Art 7(4)); where reviews are shown, how the trader checks they come from real buyers is material (Art 7(6)); search tools must explain the main ranking parameters (Art 7(4a)). (3) Annex I blacklist, unfair in all circumstances: bait advertising (point 5); ‘Falsely stating that a product will only be available for a very limited time’ (7); undisclosed paid editorial, advertorial (11); search results without ‘clearly disclosing any paid advertisement or payment specifically for achieving higher ranking’ (11a); falsely claiming a product cures illnesses (17); calling a product ‘gratis’, ‘free’, ‘without charge’ if the consumer pays anything beyond unavoidable response and delivery costs (20); falsely representing oneself as a consumer (22); claiming reviews come from real users ‘without taking reasonable and proportionate steps to check’ (23b); submitting or commissioning ‘false consumer reviews or endorsements’ or misrepresenting reviews (23c). (4) Commission guidance 2021: a ‘free’ offer may not charge for packaging, handling or administration (section 3.4); review misrepresentation includes ‘Publishing only positive reviews and deleting the negative ones’ and pre-filled positive review templates (4.2.4); influencer disclosure is inadequate as ‘hashtags at the end of a lengthy disclaimer; merely tagging a trader’ or behind ‘read more’, and free products or affiliate commission count as consideration (4.2.6). (5) From 27 Sep 2026 (2024/825 Annex): new blacklist points ban a generic environmental claim without ‘recognised excellent environmental performance relevant to the claim’ (4a), whole-product claims about one aspect (4b), offsetting-based ‘neutral, reduced or positive impact’ claims (4c) and sustainability labels not based on a certification scheme or public authority (2a). Penalty (Art 13 as amended): in coordinated cross-border enforcement the maximum fine must be ‘at least 4 % of the trader’s annual turnover in the Member State or Member States concerned’, or at least EUR 2 million where turnover data is unavailable. Related: comp:eu_prior_price_rule, comp:eu_dsa_ad_transparency, comp:uk_dmcc_schedule20, comp:ftc_consumer_reviews_rule, comp:bis_is_19000_online_reviews.

items.name: EU prior-price rule for discount copy: Price Indication Directive 98/6/EC Article 6a (inserted by Directive (EU) 2019/2161)
items.one_line: Any EU announcement of a price reduction on goods must show the trader's lowest price in at least the 30 days before the reduction, and the advertised percentage must be calculated from that prior price.

sources.title: EU Publications Office: Directive 98/6/EC (Price Indication Directive), consolidated text of 28.05.2022
sources.supports: Article 6a(1)-(5): prior price, 30-day period, Member State options for perishables, new goods, progressive reductions

sources.title: EU Publications Office: Commission Notice, Guidance on the interpretation and application of Article 6a of Directive 98/6/EC, OJ C 526, 29.12.2021
sources.supports: what counts as a price reduction announcement, goods only, worked percentage example, general announcements, loyalty and personalised discounts, interplay with the UCPD

sources.title: EU Publications Office: Judgment of the Court of Justice (Eighth Chamber), 26 September 2024, Case C-330/23
sources.supports: a percentage reduction or a promotional price statement must be determined on the basis of the prior price

sources.title: EU Publications Office: Directive (EU) 2019/2161, OJ L 328, 18.12.2019

items.note: Status as read 2026-10-13: Article 6a of Directive 98/6/EC was inserted by Directive (EU) 2019/2161, applied from 28 May 2022 (2019/2161), and is shown in the consolidated text of 28.05.2022. Text: ‘Any announcement of a price reduction shall indicate the prior price applied by the trader’ (Art 6a(1)); the prior price is the ‘lowest price applied by the trader during a period of time not shorter than 30 days prior to the application of the price reduction’ (Art 6a(2)). Exceptions are Member State options, so check the national law: different rules for ‘goods which are liable to deteriorate or expire rapidly’ (6a(3)); a shorter period where the product has been on the market for less than 30 days (6a(4)); for a progressively increased reduction, the prior price may be the price before the first reduction (6a(5)). CJEU, Case C-330/23 (a consumer association against a supermarket chain), judgment of 26 September 2024: a reduction announced ‘in the form of a percentage, or in the form of a promotional statement intended to highlight the advantageous nature of the announced price’ must be determined on the basis of the prior price. Commission guidance 2021: (1) covers ‘20 % off’, crossed-out ‘was’ prices, and announcements like ‘sales’ price, ‘special offers’ or ‘Black Friday offers’; the lowest price must include any earlier promotional price in the 30 days; worked example: ‘50 % off’ with a 30-day low of EUR 100 must show EUR 100 even though the last selling price was EUR 160. (2) Applies to goods only, not services or digital content (those stay under the UCPD), in shops and online. (3) Out of scope but still under the UCPD: ‘best/lowest prices’ claims, comparisons with recommended retail price or other sellers, tied offers like ‘buy one, get two’, genuine loyalty programmes and personalised vouchers; a discount code available to most customers is in scope. (4) A general banner (‘20 % off on everything today’) need not show the prior price on the banner, but each price tag or online price section must. (5) Extra reference prices are allowed only if clearly explained; ‘up to 70 % off’ when few items reach 70 % may breach the UCPD. Penalties are set nationally (Art 8 of the consolidated text). Related: comp:eu_ucpd.

items.name: European Accessibility Act, Directive (EU) 2019/882: accessibility requirements for products and services, incl. e-commerce, e-books, consumer banking and passenger transport information
items.one_line: Since 28 June 2025 covered products and consumer services in the EU (e-commerce sites and apps, e-books, consumer banking, passenger-transport websites, apps and tickets, telecoms, AV-media access) must be accessible, and their information must be understandable, perceivable, available as usable text and backed by text alternatives; microenterprises providing services are exempt.

sources.title: EU Publications Office: Directive (EU) 2019/882 on the accessibility requirements for products and services, OJ L 151, 7.6.2019
sources.supports: Article 2 scope and exclusions, Article 3 definitions (microenterprise, e-commerce services), Article 4(5) microenterprise exemption, Article 13 and Annex V service information, Annex I Sections I, III and IV, Article 30 penalties, Articles 31-32 application and transitional dates

items.note: Status as read 2026-10-13: in application; Member States had to adopt national laws by 28 June 2022 and ‘shall apply those measures from 28 June 2025’ (Art 31). It covers products ‘placed on the market after 28 June 2025’ and services ‘provided to consumers after 28 June 2025’ (Art 2). Transitional: service contracts agreed before 28 June 2025 may continue ‘no longer than five years from that date’, and a transitional period ends on 28 June 2030 for products already used to provide services (Art 32). Scope (Art 2): products include computers and operating systems, payment terminals, ATMs, ticketing and check-in machines, consumer terminal equipment used for electronic communications or audiovisual media, and e-readers; services include electronic communications, access to audiovisual media, websites, apps, e-tickets and travel information of air, bus, rail and waterborne passenger transport, consumer banking, ‘e-books and dedicated software’ and ‘e-commerce services’. Not covered (Art 2(4)): pre-recorded time-based media and office files published before 28 June 2025, third-party content not funded, developed or controlled by the operator, and archive content not updated after that date. Rules for a writer: (1) Service information must be made available ‘via more than one sensory channel’, ‘presented in an understandable way’, in text formats usable for assistive formats, and ‘supplementing any non-textual content with an alternative presentation’ (Annex I Section III(b)): every image, icon or video in product, help or checkout copy needs a text alternative or captions. (2) Websites and apps must be accessible by making them ‘perceivable, operable, understandable and robust’ (Section III(c)), the same four principles WCAG uses (see comp:wcag_22). (3) Consumer banking information must be understandable ‘without exceeding a level of complexity superior to level B2 (upper intermediate)’ of the CEFR (Section IV(e)). (4) E-commerce must provide ‘the information concerning accessibility of the products and services being sold’ when the responsible operator supplies it (Section IV(g)); e-books must be discoverable ‘by providing information through metadata about their accessibility features’ (Section IV(f)). (5) Service providers must explain how the service meets the requirements in ‘the general terms and conditions, or equivalent document’ (Annex V), available in written and oral format and accessibly (Art 13(2)): someone has to write an accessibility statement. (6) Product labelling, instructions and warnings must be understandable and in fonts of adequate size with sufficient contrast (Annex I Section I). Exemption: ‘Microenterprises providing services shall be exempt’ from the service accessibility requirements (Art 4(5)); a microenterprise ‘employs fewer than 10 persons’ with turnover or balance sheet not over EUR 2 million (Art 3). Penalties are set by each Member State and must be ‘effective, proportionate and dissuasive’ (Art 30). Related: comp:wcag_22, comp:rpwd_act_accessibility.

items.name: California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA) as amended by the CPRA (Proposition 24), and the California CCPA Regulations (Cal. Code Regs. tit. 11): notices, privacy policy and opt-out link wording
items.one_line: California's privacy law and its regulations fix what a business must write and where: a plain-language Notice at Collection, a privacy policy updated at least every 12 months, the exact link titles for opting out of sale/sharing and limiting sensitive data, symmetric choice wording with no dark patterns, and (from the 2025 package) a Pre-use Notice for automated decisionmaking.
aliases: Do Not Sell or Share link

sources.supports: 2025 amounts: business revenue threshold USD 26,625,000; fines not more than USD 2,663 per violation or USD 7,988 per intentional violation or violation involving known under-16s

items.note: Status as read 2026-10-13: in force. Proposition 24 (November 2020) amended the CCPA and created the California Privacy Protection Agency, now styled ‘CalPrivacy’ (cppa.ca.gov). The regulations text is marked ‘Effective 1/1/2026’. RECENT CHANGE: the 2025 package (CCPA updates, risk assessments, cybersecurity audits, automated decisionmaking technology (ADMT), insurance) was adopted on July 24, 2025 and ‘approved by the Office of Administrative Law’ on September 22, 2025, effective January 1, 2026 (ccpa_updates page); a business already using ADMT for a significant decision must comply with the ADMT article ‘no later than January 1, 2027’ (regulations Article 11). A ‘Notices & Disclosures’ pre-rulemaking topic closed for comment on May 20, 2026 and is not yet a proposal. Rules for a writer: (1) Every disclosure must be ‘easy to read and understandable’ and ‘use plain, straightforward language and avoid technical or legal jargon’ (reg 7003(a)); readable on small screens, in the languages the business normally uses with Californians, and reasonably accessible to people with disabilities, following standards such as WCAG 2.1 for online notices (7003(b)). (2) Notice at Collection, at or before the point of collection: the categories of personal information (incl. sensitive), purposes, whether each category is sold or shared, how long each is kept or the criteria, the opt-out link and a privacy-policy link (7012(e)); a link must land on the exact section, not the top of the policy (7012(f)); ‘the business shall not collect’ without it (7012(d)). (3) Privacy policy: online and offline practices, categories collected in the preceding 12 months, sources, purposes, what is sold or shared and to whom, every CCPA right, how to exercise it, and the ‘Date the privacy policy was last updated’ (7011(e)), behind a conspicuous link using the word ‘privacy’ (7011(d)); the statute requires updating ‘at least once every 12 months’ (Civil Code 1798.130(a)(5)). (4) Exact link titles: “Do Not Sell or Share My Personal Information” and “Limit the Use of My Sensitive Personal Information” (Civil Code 1798.135(a)), in the homepage header or footer (7013(c), 7014(c)); or one link titled ‘Your Privacy Choices’ or ‘Your California Privacy Choices’ with the opt-out icon beside it (7015(b)); links at least the size and colour of neighbouring links (7003(c)). (5) Choice wording must be symmetrical: ‘Accept All’ with ‘Decline All’, not only ‘More Information’; ‘Yes’ with ‘No’, not ‘Ask me later’; no double negatives such as Yes/No beside a do-not-sell statement; no false-urgency countdowns (7004(a)); consent obtained by a dark pattern ‘shall not constitute consumer consent’ (7004(b)). (6) ADMT Pre-use Notice: a ‘plain language explanation of the specific purpose’, never just ‘to make a significant decision’ (7220(c)(1)); the site must display whether an opt-out preference signal was honoured, e.g. ‘Opt-Out Request Honored’ (7025(c)(6)). Penalty: fines adjusted for 2025 to not more than USD 2,663 per violation or USD 7,988 per intentional violation or violation involving known under-16s (cpi_adjustment page). Other US state privacy laws: not read in this pass. Related: comp:gdpr_marketing_consent, comp:coppa, comp:wcag_22, comp:ccpa_dark_patterns_2023 (India's CCPA, a different body).
